1.title: Commission explicitly includes Schengen in Cyprus's preparations
1.summary: In its regular report, the Commission called for adoption of the Schengen visa system, document checks aligned with the Schengen Convention and preparation of government computer networks for SIS. Personal data protection remained a separate area of work.
1.impact: This is a documented starting point for the timeline: substantive preparation was under way by 1999. The report does not establish the date of the first political discussion.
1.provenance: 1999 Regular Report on Cyprus’ progress towards accession, cover date 13.10.1999, printed pp. 39–40 and 57–58. The footer ‘First Draft 06/10/99’ refers to an internal version of the text.

2.title: Justice and home affairs negotiating chapter opens
2.summary: Chapter 24 of Cyprus's EU accession negotiations opened. It included Schengen rules on borders, visas, data protection and police cooperation. The European Parliament separately explained that EU accession would not automatically remove checks: a subsequent unanimous Council decision would be needed.
2.impact: Formal negotiations began on the package that included Schengen. This was part of the EU membership negotiations, rather than a separate decision on Schengen accession.
2.provenance: European Parliament, Cyprus — Chapter 24, WIP/2002/11/0037, p. 1; a retrospective factsheet after the negotiations ended. It gives the opening month, without a day.

3.title: Cyprus adopts a Schengen Action Plan
3.summary: Cyprus approved a plan to implement Schengen rules. Plans for Larnaca and Paphos airports were changed to separate passenger flows, and equipment to detect forged documents was installed in the summer. National SIS equipment, coastal radar, patrol boats and helicopters were planned for 2001–2002.
3.impact: Preparation gained a specific plan and infrastructure tasks. The future purchases listed in the report did not yet represent completed work.
3.provenance: European Commission, SEC(2001)1745, report dated 13.11.2001, printed p. 79.

4.title: Chapter 24 is provisionally closed
4.summary: The justice and home affairs negotiating chapter was provisionally closed. In the final factsheet after the negotiations ended, its final status is dated December 2002. No transitional periods were provided for the chapter.
4.impact: The parties agreed the EU accession terms for this chapter. Removing checks between Cyprus and Schengen countries remained a separate future stage.
4.provenance: European Parliament, WIP/2002/11/0037, p. 1; the document gives both closure dates.

5.title: Commission records SIS delays and port-control problems
5.summary: The regular report confirmed implementation of the Schengen Action Plan and airport preparations. Developments in SIS II were delaying some IT measures. Embarkation and disembarkation procedures at seaports still did not fully ensure the required individual checks on people crossing the border.
5.impact: Having a plan did not mean readiness was complete. Preparation already depended on infrastructure, IT and the work of border services together.
5.provenance: European Commission, SEC(2002)1401, 09.10.2002, printed pp. 104 and 131. The dates for future terminals in the document were plans at that time.

6.title: Accession treaty establishes a two-stage Schengen model
6.summary: Article 3 of the Act of Accession provided for some Schengen provisions to apply from EU membership. The remaining provisions also became binding, but their application required a separate Council decision after verification of the conditions and consultation of the European Parliament.
6.impact: The legal basis for later accession was established. The treaty set no calendar deadline for removing checks.
6.provenance: 2003 Act of Accession, Article 3; the treaty was signed on 16.04.2003 and published in OJ L236 on 23.09.2003.

7.title: Pre-accession monitoring leaves SIS, airport and data-protection tasks
7.summary: The final monitoring report assessed preparation under the plan as satisfactory for EU accession. Integration into SIS II, separation of passenger flows at airports and ports, and strengthening the Data Protection Commissioner's office still remained.
7.impact: The Commission distinguished readiness for EU membership from meeting the conditions for future removal of internal checks.
7.provenance: European Commission, SEC(2003)1202 final, Chapter 24; European Parliament register giving the report date as 05.11.2003.

8.title: Council establishes a special Green Line regime
8.summary: Regulation 866/2004 was adopted on movement of people and goods across the line between government-controlled areas and areas outside its effective control. It took effect on 1 May. The Green Line was not recognised as an ordinary EU external border.
8.impact: A special legal regime was created that must be taken into account in the island's Schengen integration.
8.provenance: Regulation 866/2004, corrected official text, adopted 29.04.2004; corrected publication 09.06.2004. European Commission explanation.

9.title: Cyprus joins the EU with border checks retained
9.summary: Cyprus became an EU member, and the Act of Accession obligations took effect. Full application of the Schengen package and removal of the relevant checks remained subject to a separate procedure.
9.impact: EU membership did not mean automatic entry into the area without internal border checks.
9.provenance: Act of Accession, Article 3; European Parliament, 2012 overview, p. 24.

10.title: Early readiness declaration opens a partial evaluation
10.summary: Cyprus's declaration was registered as 7555/05 SCHEVAL18 COMIX192. It allowed evaluation to start from 1 May 2006, with airports, seaports and visa issuance deferred. On-site inspections of police cooperation and data protection took place.
10.impact: Official Schengen evaluation existed long before 2019. The date 1 May refers to the start of the early stage, rather than completion of the inspections.
10.provenance: Council of the EU, ST 14518/2/06 REV 2, 20.11.2006, paragraphs 10–11. The public copy was declassified in 2018; that is the disclosure date of an older source. The exact submission day of the 2005 declaration is not established in this entry.

11.title: Draft conclusions list problems after the early inspections
11.summary: The draft recorded that sea and air border evaluations had not yet taken place. The data protection authority lacked resources and experience with SIS, and a revisit was needed. Database and SIRENE bureau tasks remained in police cooperation.
11.impact: Progress was partial. The document cannot be presented as an accession decision or finally adopted Council conclusions.
11.provenance: ST 14518/2/06 REV 2, 20.11.2006, pp. 3–4. Wording in other draft versions on the ‘border issue’ does not establish a legal requirement to reunify the island first.

12.title: Commission links Green Line surveillance to future Schengen participation
12.summary: In its Green Line report, the Commission urged Cyprus to fulfil its surveillance obligations with future Schengen participation in mind. At the same time, it maintained the approach of avoiding excessive obstacles to contacts between communities and not treating the line as an EU external border.
12.impact: The practical question of monitoring the line was already on the official agenda at an early stage.

13.title: Council admits nine countries from the 2004 enlargement, excluding Cyprus
13.summary: Decision 2007/801/EC extended full application of the rules to Czechia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Hungary, Malta, Poland, Slovenia and Slovakia. Land and sea checks were to end on 21 December 2007 and air checks on 30 March 2008. Cyprus was not listed.
13.impact: Cyprus's path diverged from that of the other nine countries that joined the EU in 2004. Its absence from the list alone establishes neither a single cause of delay nor a veto by any country.

14.title: New evaluation mechanism provides a transition period for Cyprus
14.summary: Regulation 1053/2013 replaced the previous Schengen evaluation mechanism. It expressly recognised that Cyprus's evaluation had already begun under the old rules and deferred application of the new mechanism to Cyprus until 1 January 2016.
14.impact: This provides the legal link between the early inspections and the modern procedure, rather than a new decision to admit Cyprus to Schengen.
14.provenance: Regulation 1053/2013, recital 27 and Article 23; adopted 07.10.2013, published 06.11.2013.

15.title: Commission awaits notification to evaluate all relevant areas
15.summary: In its communication on strengthening Schengen, the Commission said it would evaluate Cyprus in all relevant areas after receiving notification from the country.
15.impact: At that point, full up-to-date confirmation of readiness was still absent. The next substantial milestone was the 2019 declaration.
15.provenance: European Commission, COM(2017)570 final, 27.09.2017, printed p. 13.

16.title: Cyprus confirms readiness for full Schengen evaluation
16.summary: Cyprus declared its intention to apply all parts of the Schengen rules and undergo evaluations, taking account of the island's special circumstances under Protocol No 10.
16.impact: The current cycle began. Calling this the country's first Schengen application would be inaccurate.

17.title: Commission adds Cyprus to evaluation programmes
17.summary: Through Decisions C(2019)7326 and C(2019)7278, the Commission amended the evaluation programmes to include Cyprus for 2019–2020.
17.impact: The country's declaration moved into a scheduled inspection procedure.

18.title: Data protection evaluation takes place
18.summary: Experts assessed Cyprus's compliance with Schengen personal data protection requirements. The result became a prerequisite for processing real SIS data.
18.impact: A specific area was assessed. Passing it did not replace the evaluation of visas, borders and policing.
18.provenance: Council Decision 2023/870, recital 3; adopted 25.04.2023, published 28.04.2023, and describing the evaluation retrospectively.

19.title: Commission confirms that data protection conditions are met
19.summary: Following a positive opinion from the Schengen Committee, report C(2020)8150 was adopted, confirming that the necessary data protection conditions had been met.
19.impact: A necessary stage for SIS was passed. Recommendations for further improvements remained.
19.provenance: COM(2021)472 final, 12.08.2021, p. 1, giving the decision date of 05.11.2020.

20.title: National SIS technical readiness is confirmed
20.summary: The SIS II Advisory Group confirmed the national system's readiness for integration, based on eu-LISA test report 2020-377.
20.impact: Testing was completed before legal authorisation and the actual SIS launch in July 2023.

21.title: Council adopts data protection recommendations
21.summary: The Council adopted 17 recommendations covering supervisory authority resources, citizens' rights, SIS/VIS legislation, operation logs, security and data quality. Cyprus had three months to produce an action plan.
21.impact: The positive 2020 evaluation came with specific remedial tasks. The full accession procedure continued.
21.provenance: ST 5535/21, decision adopted by written procedure on 21.01.2021; final document dated 25.01.2021.

22.title: Experts evaluate external borders and police cooperation
22.summary: Two main operational areas were evaluated. The results were recorded in report C(2021)3600 on borders and C(2021)3500 on police cooperation.
22.impact: The deficiencies identified formed the basis of Council recommendations in autumn 2021.
22.provenance: ST 12639/21, borders, paragraph 1; ST 12638/21, police, paragraph 1. Both documents were issued on 08.10.2021.

23.title: Commission proposes authorising SIS use
23.summary: Proposal COM(2021)472 was submitted under file 2021/0266(NLE). It established a legal path towards using real SIS data.
23.impact: The proposal did not yet grant system access or remove border checks.
23.provenance: COM(2021)472 final; European Parliament legislative procedure entry, 12.08.2021.

24.title: Council adopts recommendations on return procedures
24.summary: Eleven recommendations were adopted on return procedures, decisions, appeals, detention and monitoring of forced return. A remedial action plan was required within three months.
24.impact: A formal task list was established for one area of the initial evaluation.
24.provenance: ST 12636/21, adopted 07.10.2021, document dated 08.10.2021. Sources disagree on the month of the preceding evaluation: COM(2021)472 gives November 2020, while this act gives December; no separate exact visit date is asserted here.

25.title: Council sets police cooperation tasks
25.summary: Nine recommendations covered information exchange and police databases. Priorities included a single 24/7 contact point, automated information processing and officers' mobile access to data.
25.impact: Readiness required working day-to-day information exchange procedures alongside changes to legislation.

26.title: Council adopts external border recommendations
26.summary: Eighteen recommendations were adopted on border management, risk analysis, staff training, EUROSUR, maritime surveillance and checks. Human resources were identified as a priority.
26.impact: Specific operational conditions were set for further preparation. An action plan was required within three months.

27.title: Common visa policy evaluation takes place
27.summary: Experts evaluated Cyprus's visa procedures. The results were recorded in report C(2022)960 and formed the basis of the 2022 recommendations.
27.impact: The evaluation covered consular practice and IT needed to apply common visa rules.
27.provenance: ST 10403/22, 17.06.2022, paragraph 1 gives the exact visit dates.

28.title: Cyprus submits border and return action plans
28.summary: The external border plan was sent on 25 January and the return plan on 31 January. Both addressed the Council's 2021 recommendations.
28.impact: The process moved from identifying deficiencies to assessing proposed measures.
28.provenance: COM(2022)192, ST 8936/22, Commission communication dated 03.05.2022; partially disclosed to the public on 27.03.2024.

29.title: Commission assesses plans but requests clarification
29.summary: The return and border plans were found broadly adequate. Further detail was needed for some measures: certain points repeated recommendations without sufficiently describing specific actions.
29.impact: An adequate plan did not mean that all deficiencies had been remedied.

30.title: European Parliament supports the SIS proposal
30.summary: The European Parliament approved the proposal by 403 votes to 58, with 69 abstentions. This was a consultative opinion for a subsequent Council decision.
30.impact: The parliamentary stage was completed. Access to the system did not take effect that day.
30.provenance: European Parliament, vote result and decision summary, 03.05.2022.

31.title: Council adopts 42 visa policy recommendations
31.summary: The recommendations covered fingerprints, visa IT, application forms, stickers, training, honorary consuls and the pro-visa procedure. Three months were allowed for an action plan.
31.impact: Preparation required changes in consular practice and technology. These requirements describe the evaluation in 2022, rather than automatically representing the rules for applicants today.

32.title: Visa plan is submitted and its adequacy assessed
32.summary: Council working party materials list Cyprus's visa plan dated 23 September 2022 and a document assessing its adequacy dated 27 February 2023.
32.impact: A follow-up process is confirmed. Document titles do not establish that all visa recommendations had already been implemented.
32.provenance: Council of the EU, working party materials for 7 March 2023.

33.title: Working party agrees the draft SIS decision
33.summary: The Working Party for Schengen Matters, with associated countries participating, agreed the draft. Coreper endorsement and Council adoption were to follow.
33.impact: The file moved towards adoption of the act, but working-level agreement did not itself open the system.
33.provenance: ST 8181/1/23 REV 1, paragraph 8, retrospective description of the meeting on 07.03.2023.

34.title: Council adopts decision applying SIS provisions
34.summary: Decision 2023/870 was adopted. It provided for preparatory data transfer from 13 June and application of the relevant SIS rules from 25 July. Special restrictions remained until internal border checks were lifted.
34.impact: This was legal authorisation for SIS integration. Full accession required a different decision.
34.provenance: Council Decision 2023/870, adopted 25.04.2023, published 28.04.2023, entered into force 29.04.2023.

35.title: Authorised SIS data transfer date arrives
35.summary: From this date, the decision allowed SIS alerts, supplementary information and data to be made available to Cyprus. The main powers to use the system and enter its own alerts began on 25 July.
35.impact: This was an intermediate legal launch date. It does not itself establish the exact day when each dataset was actually transferred.
35.grade_note: A, stage provided for in the act

36.title: Cyprus connects to SIS in practice
36.summary: Cypriot authorities began using SIS and entering their own alerts. The system enabled information exchange on wanted and missing people, certain categories of third-country nationals and stolen objects.
36.impact: Practical integration into shared information exchange began. The Interior Ministry separately explained that border checks remained.
36.provenance: eu-LISA, Cyprus fully integrated into SIS; European Commission in Cyprus; clarification by Cyprus's Interior Ministry, 25.07.2023.

37.title: Practical SIS use is evaluated
37.summary: Following connection, the first evaluation of SIS application in Cyprus took place. The results were recorded in report C(2024)700. The Council later identified the SIRENE training centre and its set of instructions as good practice, but retained a list of improvements.
37.impact: Launching the system made it possible to evaluate its actual use; technical connection did not complete the evaluation.
37.provenance: ST 11237/24, document dated 14.06.2024, paragraph 1 gives the visit dates.

38.title: Commission reviews the first SIS results
38.summary: The State of Schengen Report 2024 noted good integration of SIS into Cyprus's border, migration and police processes, but incomplete use of its potential. Since connection, about 20 people wanted under European Arrest Warrants had been arrested; roughly three quarters had been surrendered to the requesting states.
38.impact: Measurable results of cooperation emerged. They did not mean preparation was complete in all areas.

39.title: Council calls for improvements to SIS use
39.summary: The recommendations called for strengthening SIRENE, enabling the required alert categories, ensuring complete available data and object searches, and improving fingerprint use. An action plan was expected within two months, followed by reports every six months and a verification visit before closure.
39.impact: Specific tasks on practical SIS use remained after connection.
39.provenance: ST 11237/24, file 2024/0105(NLE), decision adopted 13.06.2024, final document dated 14.06.2024.

40.title: Government reviews action plans across six areas
40.summary: The Foreign Ministry held an interministerial meeting on data protection, police cooperation, borders, return, visas and SIS. Interior, justice, transport and migration authorities took part, and urgent tasks were identified.
40.impact: Work continued across all evaluated areas. The announcement did not declare the plans closed.
40.provenance: Cyprus Foreign Ministry, announcement on the interministerial meeting; event and publication 19.12.2024.

41.title: President sets a 2025 technical readiness target
41.summary: At the Beyond Sea & Sun forum, Nikos Christodoulides announced a Foreign Ministry working group and the intention to meet technical conditions during 2025. In his assessment, political concerns related to the ceasefire line had been addressed.
41.impact: The official text promised technical readiness in 2025. This was not a Council decision on accession in the same year.
41.provenance: Cyprus Presidency, address at Beyond Sea & Sun; event and publication 10.01.2025.

42.title: Commission confirms the initial evaluation is continuing
42.summary: In a reply to the European Parliament, Commissioner Magnus Brunner said Cyprus's initial Schengen evaluation was continuing. A positive result and a unanimous Council decision would be required, taking account of the island's special circumstances under Protocol No 10.
42.impact: In spring 2025, the Commission had not yet declared the technical evaluation complete.
42.provenance: European Parliament, reply to E-000502/2025, dated 16.04.2025, answering the question submitted on 05.02.2025.

43.title: Commission sets out a conditional path to verification visits
43.summary: The State of Schengen Report 2025 noted improvements in return and SIS, but kept the initial evaluation open. Verification visits in 2025 depended on the necessary remedial work being completed beforehand.
43.impact: A conditional route towards confirming readiness was published, without setting an accession date.
43.provenance: European Commission, COM(2025)185 final with annexes, 23.04.2025.

44.title: Cabinet approves a VIS bill
44.summary: The Council of Ministers approved a bill on the operation and use of the Visa Information System. It defined the national system, authorities' powers, access, application of visa rules, penalties and appeals.
44.impact: Legislative preparation in the visa area advanced. Cabinet approval did not amount to parliamentary enactment or a confirmed launch of the European VIS.
44.provenance: Official portal for the Cyprus government's programme, 08.05.2025.

45.title: President names 2026 as the accession year
45.summary: Christodoulides expressed confidence in accession in 2026. He expected technical preparations to be completed by the end of 2025, while seeking support from other countries and the European Parliament.
45.impact: This statement named the accession year, whereas the January statement concerned technical readiness. The target imposed no binding deadline on the Council of the EU.
45.provenance: CyBC, report dated 11.05.2025; CNA via StockWatch, English publication dated 12.05.2025 on the previous day's statement.

46.title: Commission monitors readiness
46.summary: Monitoring activities assessed Cyprus's readiness after remedial work. They later formed the basis of the 2025/2026 country report adopted in July 2026.
46.impact: This was actual verification following work on the recommendations. The primary sources cited do not give exact days, so the event is dated by month.
46.provenance: COM(2026)150 final, section 3.3, 18.05.2026; European Commission briefing, 15.07.2026.

47.title: France and Cyprus prepare future consular representation
47.summary: A letter of intent was signed in Paris for France to represent Cyprus in consular matters after full accession, where Cyprus has no presence of its own. The President thanked France for supporting accession in 2026.
47.impact: A basis was prepared for future visa cooperation. The letter did not replace the readiness evaluation or the Council decision.
47.provenance: Cyprus Presidency, announcement on the strategic partnership and Letter of Intent, event dated 15.12.2025; Greek announcement on the same day.

48.title: Christodoulides retains the 2026 accession target
48.summary: At a joint press conference with Ursula von der Leyen, the President said readiness for full accession had been discussed and expressed an expectation of accession during the year.
48.impact: The political goal remained after the December monitoring. The President's statement alone does not mean the Commission had agreed a legal date.
48.provenance: Cyprus Presidency, statement at the joint press conference, 15.01.2026.

49.title: Brunner expects evaluation report adoption in spring
49.summary: In an interview with CNA, the Commissioner reported substantial progress and expected the report to be adopted in spring 2026. Once readiness was confirmed, the Council would need to decide on accession unanimously.
49.impact: Spring was the expected timing of a procedural step. Actual adoption of the report is confirmed on 14 July.
49.provenance: CNA via ABNA-SE, Brunner interview, publication dated 23.01.2026; the exact recording day is not given.

50.title: Commission officially notes progress made in 2025
50.summary: The State of Schengen Report 2026 confirmed substantial reforms in Cyprus and the December monitoring. Full accession remained an area of further EU work.
50.impact: This was a positive assessment of progress in the general Schengen report. It preceded the separate country report on Cyprus.

51.title: President shifts expected political decision to late 2026 or early 2027
51.summary: Christodoulides reported substantial progress and said a political decision was expected in late 2026 or early 2027.
51.impact: The public target became more cautious than the promise of accession in 2026. The political decision date and the date checks are actually removed may differ.
51.provenance: Cyprus Presidency, statement of 21 May; KNEWS, report dated 21.05.2026.

52.title: Schengen Committee gives a positive opinion
52.summary: Member states in the Schengen Committee gave a positive opinion on Cyprus's country report. The Commission later explicitly named this date at a briefing.
52.impact: A stage preceding Commission adoption of the report was completed. This was not a unanimous Council decision removing checks.
52.provenance: European Commission, briefing dated 15.07.2026, SCHENGEN — Cyprus section, retrospectively describing the opinion of 26.06.2026.

53.title: Commission adopts a positive country report
53.summary: The Schengen Country Report of Cyprus 2025/2026 was adopted. According to the Commission, it is based on monitoring in December 2025 and gives a positive assessment of Cyprus's technical preparedness. The report was sent to the Council and the European Parliament.
53.impact: The file advanced towards Council consideration. The Commission separately stressed that decisions on when and how accession takes place belong to the Council.
53.provenance: Commission briefing dated 15.07.2026; ST 13022/26 entry referring to C(2026)3652. The September dates in the entries concern transmission of the materials, not the report's adoption in July.

54.title: Country report appears in Council working party materials
54.summary: Materials for the Working Party for Schengen Matters included the Commission decision establishing the country report. ST 13022/26 is dated 14 September in the Council register; the meeting was scheduled for the 15th.
54.impact: The document's progress into Council working bodies is confirmed. Inclusion in the materials alone does not establish adoption of a final decision.
54.provenance: Council of the EU, meeting of 15.09.2026; register entry for ST 13022/26.

55.title: Cyprus says Commission recommendations have been implemented
55.summary: Nicholas Ioannides said the Commission's recommendations were considered implemented, Cyprus was technically ready and political agreement was now needed.
55.impact: This was the government's official position. It cannot be substituted for an adopted Council act closing the action plans.
55.provenance: EUAA, account of the statement with an event date of 01.10.2026; Cyprus government announcement. The government announcement was published on 02.10.2026.

56.title: Report on implementation of remedial action plans is prepared
56.summary: The ST 13957/26 entry describes an assessment of implementation of plans addressing deficiencies identified in the 2021/2022/2023 initial evaluation. Access to the full text is restricted.
56.impact: Formal monitoring of the plans is confirmed. The title does not establish the outcome of each recommendation.
56.provenance: Austrian Parliament, ST 13957/26: created 04.10.2026, received by Parliament 09.10.2026. This differs from 5 October in the site's earlier selection; the creation date in the official entry is used here.
56.grade_note: A, metadata for a restricted document

57.title: MED9 supports Cyprus's progress
57.summary: In the Split Declaration, MED9 countries welcomed the positive outcome of the 2025/2026 country report and the start of Council discussions. They called for timely completion of the remaining steps.
57.impact: Collective political support was recorded. This wording set no specific accession date.
57.provenance: Full text of the Split Declaration, 07.10.2026, Migration and Protection of the EU’s External Borders section; excerpts published by the Cyprus Presidency.

58.title: Minister describes six remaining actions
58.summary: In a CyBC interview, Ioannides expected six remaining actions to be completed by early November and full accession in 2027. The plan was then to notify the Commission and proceed through the subsequent institutional steps.
58.impact: The statement clarifies the authorities' plan, but differs from the 1 October wording on how complete the work was. Six actions cannot automatically be equated with the six evaluation areas.

59.title: Draft closure of action plans in six areas is registered
59.summary: ST 14872/26 appeared in the Council register under file 2026/0337(NLE). The proposal concerns closure of plans on data protection, return, external borders, police, visas and SIS. The text is restricted.
59.impact: The Commission proposed completing monitoring of the remedial plans. Registration of the proposal does not establish adoption and does not replace the decision on full Schengen application.
59.provenance: Council of the EU, register entry for ST 14872/26, 27.10.2026.

60.title: Action plan closure appears on the working party agenda
60.summary: The agenda included Commission presentation of draft ST 14872/26, discussion and possible agreement. Separate updates from the Commission and Cyprus on full application of Schengen rules were also scheduled.
60.impact: The planned subject of discussion is confirmed. ‘Possible agreement’ does not mean agreement was reached.
60.provenance: CM 4752/1/26 REV 1, agenda issued 11.11.2026; item 5 concerns the meeting of 13.11.2026.

61.title: Commission and Cyprus presentations are issued
61.summary: Working document WK 17427/26 contains presentations on Cyprus's 2025/2026 evaluation for the 13 November meeting. The full text is marked LIMITE.
61.impact: The entry confirms that meeting materials exist, but does not disclose whether agreement on the proposal was reached.
61.provenance: Austrian Parliament, WK 17427/26: meeting on 13.11.2026, document created 17.11.2026, received by Parliament 18.11.2026. The entry date is not replaced by the meeting date here.

62.title: Greek Prime Minister supports the 1 July 2027 target
62.summary: In Nicosia, Kyriakos Mitsotakis expressed hope for Cyprus's formal accession on 1 July, at the start of Greece's Council presidency in the second half of 2027.
62.impact: A specific target gained public backing from Athens. In the transcript, it is an expectation rather than an announcement of an adopted Council decision.
62.provenance: Official transcript from the Greek Prime Minister; event and publication 18.11.2026.

63.title: Initial December Council agenda does not schedule a Cyprus decision
63.summary: CM 4999/26 for the Council on 3–4 December lists Schengen governance issues, but no separate adoption of a Cyprus accession decision. Information item ST 15799/26 appeared later.
63.impact: The initial agenda did not confirm an accession vote. Its contents could change before the meeting.

64.title: EU and UK reaffirm work on the bases protocol
64.summary: The summit's joint statement committed to completing implementation of the protocol on the British Sovereign Base Areas in Cyprus in all its parts.
64.impact: This matters for the island's special arrangements. The statement establishes neither separate arrangements for Schengen checks at crossing points nor Cyprus's accession date.

65.title: Tender opens for passport-control booths in Larnaca and Paphos
65.summary: Tender MTCW/AIR2/BOOTHS/2026 was published with an estimated value of €440,000 and a 21 December submission deadline. Philenews reported 22 booths and eight months for manufacture, installation and testing after contract signature. The procurement entry gives an overall contract duration of 20 months.
65.impact: The tender confirms further infrastructure upgrades. The different periods refer to different descriptions of the work; no link between completion and a mandatory accession date has been established.
65.provenance: Official tender entry, published 20.11.2026 at 15:29; Philenews, description of equipment and work stages, 25.11.2026.

66.title: Commission prepares an information item for the December Council
66.summary: ST 15799/26 concerns the Justice and Home Affairs Council meeting on 3–4 December and is titled as an update on the application of the Schengen acquis in Cyprus. It is listed under Any Other Business. Access to the text is restricted.
66.impact: Preparation of a briefing for ministers is confirmed. An information item is not a draft decision on full accession and does not itself confirm a vote.
66.provenance: Austrian Parliament, ST 15799/26: created 22.11.2026, received by Parliament 23.11.2026.
66.grade_note: A, metadata for a restricted document
